1.0.0.en: St. Paul speaks as a Jew to his brethren the Hebrew Jews about the fathers of the Jewish people in the Old Testament, and how God's word came to them through the prophets.

1.0.1.en: In many kinds and ways: visions, dreams, appearances, and symbols of every sort, such as sacrifices and the like, and the Law with its commandments.

1.0.2.en: In this he shows the unity of the two Testaments: God is the One who speaks in the Old Testament through the prophets, and in the New Testament through Christ incarnate. And in order to show the superiority of Christ over the prophets, he confirms the Jews who had become Christians in their faith in the face of the doubts raised by their Jewish brethren and their exclusion of them from entering the Temple. So he shows that the Old Testament was a preparation for the New Testament, and that the symbols are done away with by the coming of the One they symbolize, who is greater than all the means of the Old Testament for revealing God.

1.1.0.en: These last days: that is, the New Testament.

1.1.1.en: Whom he hath appointed heir of all things: he declared that He is the owner of all things, for He is the Creator and the Redeemer who bought us with His blood, and by His perfect righteousness He became the perfect image of man as man ought to be. The ownership of the Son is equal to the ownership of the Father, which Christ Himself declared when He said, “All things that the Father hath are mine” (Jn 16:15). By whom also he made the worlds: this shows the eternity of the Son, who at the appointed time created the worlds, the world of heaven and the world of earth.

1.1.2.en: It shows the superiority and distinction of the New Testament, since the means of speaking to mankind is no longer the prophets but God Himself incarnate, who created all creatures and then became incarnate in the fullness of time, and by His righteousness and redemption all creation became subject to Him, just as God wanted Adam to have dominion over all creation in Paradise.

1.2.1.en: The brightness of his glory: Christ is the light of the Father, for He is Light from Light. This is a proof of the divinity of Christ, because there is no glory without brightness; He is eternal like the eternity of the glory, and does not come after it in time, as some who doubt the divinity of Christ claim.

1.2.2.en: The express image of his person: another proof of the divinity of Christ, for the image and form of God's essence appeared in the incarnate Christ; He is the very essence of God, appearing in visible form to mankind in the fullness of time. The image is not something else, or separate, or lesser, as those who use this verse to cast doubt on the divinity of Christ claim, but is the manifestation of the essence of God to mankind, as the Scripture says, “No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him” (Jn 1:18). Upholding all things: that is, the Lord Christ is the Sustainer of all things and the One who cares for them; He holds them in His hands and governs them, for He is not only their Creator but their Governor as well.

1.2.3.en: By the word of his power: His wisdom, which created all creatures, is able to do all things and governs the whole. When he had by himself purged our sins: He accomplished redemption Himself in order to cleanse all who believe in Him from their sins; He is the One who works by Himself in the New Testament, and not through another, as in the Old Testament.

1.2.4.en: Sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high: the right hand represents blessing and power, and does not mean a particular direction, because God is unlimited and has neither right nor left. What is meant is that Christ, after His resurrection, ascended into the heavens to be in His glory which He had from eternity and which He hid by His incarnation and humility in order to accomplish our redemption; that is, the divine majesty became manifest to mankind in the heights, that is, the heavens, which is everything that is exalted above our minds and our material thoughts.

1.2.5.en: St. Paul continues his discourse about Christ, who is God, the Creator and Governor of all that exists, and who became incarnate and emptied Himself in order to accomplish the redemption of mankind, and then ascended into heaven. In this the greatness of Christ and of Christianity appears over Judaism, which symbolizes it and prepares the way for it.

1.2.6.en: God desires to speak with you always, and in His wisdom He seeks the way by which you will respond, whether through events around you, or people close to you, or His voice in the Holy Bible, so that you may repent and return to Him; and out of His abundant love He gives you Himself in His Body and Blood on the altar. So do you, beloved, enjoy these revelations that call you to His embrace, or do you still think of God as an obscure God, incomprehensible, far from you and set apart in His heaven?

1.3.0.en: Being made: this does not mean change, but that Christ, after accomplishing redemption, regained His glory which He had voluntarily set aside.

1.3.1.en: Inherited: this indicates that the Lord Christ possesses all the authority that God the Father has (Jn 3:35). Name: standing.

1.3.2.en: By the ascension of Christ His eternal divine glory appeared, which is greater than the glory of the angels whom He created in heaven, for He is God, the Owner of all creatures, whereas the angels possess superior abilities in understanding, movement and work which God gave them.

1.4.0.en: Unto which of: a style that denies with all certainty that any of the angels is equal to the Lord Christ, to Him be glory, and this refutes the doctrine of the Adventists or the Jehovah's Witnesses that the Lord Christ is the angel Michael. This day: what is meant is before all ages.

1.4.1.en: Here he speaks of the eternity of the Son, begotten of the Father before all ages, quoting this from (Ps 2:7) and also (Ps 89:26, 27). He is equal to the Father in essence, whereas the angels are creatures whom God created at a particular time, just as He created the rest of mankind. And of course our sonship to God by adoption is different from the Son's sonship to the Father in essence.

1.5.0.en: And again, when he bringeth in: the Father sent the Son and brought Him into the world by the Incarnation. This does not mean the separation of the Father from the Son, for they are one in essence, and this is a movement within the divine Self, just as a man sends from his mind a signal to one of his members, such as his hand or his foot, to move; he is not two but one man.

1.5.1.en: The firstbegotten: the Divine inspiration, through the tongue of St. Paul, means that when the Son became incarnate and entered into the world, He set aside the glory that was His. Therefore he used the word firstborn, which indicates that Christ as man is the firstborn of all who believe in Him; He is the God who became man, who presented to us the new man in place of fallen Adam. This of course does not mean that He is merely a created man, but that in His humility He became incarnate to become, by His pure human nature, the firstborn for everyone who believes in Him; and He is the firstborn of creation, that is, its head, and not the first created.

1.5.2.en: Let all the angels of God worship him: the Divine inspiration brought this testimony from (the Book of Deuteronomy 32:43) according to the Septuagint translation of the Holy Bible, confirming that the angels worship the Son, for it is self-evident that the One worshipped is greater than the one who offers worship.

1.5.3.en: The distinction of Christ from the angels appears in that when He became incarnate the angels worshipped Him, because they know that He is God, their Creator and the Creator of all that exists.

1.6.0.en: Winds: as a comparison, that they are an instrument in the hand of God which He uses for His will, and they (the angels) are not themselves merely wind (Jon 1:4). A flame of fire: because they are spirits kindled with the fire of divine love, he likens them to a flame of fire; and what is meant is what he mentioned, that they are servants and instruments in His divine hand.

1.6.1.en: St. Paul brought comparisons for the angels which he took from (Ps 104:4), namely the winds and the flame of fire, to declare that both are creatures created by the Son, like the angels, to affirm that the angels are created and are not like the Son, of whom he says, “Thy throne, O God”...

1.7.0.en: Thy throne: your throne, and the meaning of the verse is that your kingdom is everlasting forever.

1.7.1.en: A sceptre: the sceptre of rule, and the meaning is that the order of your kingdom is uprightness.

1.7.2.en: On the other hand he shows that Christ is God, the King of kings, who rules the whole world forever, and the angels are merely His servants, as (Ps 45:6) mentions.

1.8.0.en: Thou hast loved righteousness, and hated iniquity: righteousness is a constant attribute in the Lord Christ, which does not change in Him and which He does not lose for any reason, because it is not given to Him by another, like the angels, whose righteousness is given by God, and the proof of this is the fall of a number of the angels who became demons (Jude 6). God hath anointed thee: its meaning is that He set you apart to accomplish redemption.

1.8.1.en: Thy God: with respect to the humanity.

1.8.2.en: Above thy fellows: all the anointed kings and prophets; and he means in general all creatures, whom He became incarnate to resemble in everything except sin.

1.8.3.en: Kings used to be anointed with oil, and each one of them who was anointed was called “the Lord's anointed.” The phrase above thy fellows here means the distinction of our Lord Jesus Christ from all the kings and prophets who came before Him, as (Ps 45:7) mentions. They are His fellows with respect to the mission of preaching, warning and proclaiming the voice of God, but the special anointing of Christ relates to His redemption and His salvation of us, which no one else can accomplish, because He is distinguished from all mankind and the angels by perfect righteousness and perfect joy; He is the source of all joy in the world for all creatures, whether angels or men.

1.8.4.en: Do you love righteousness, so that you strive to acquire the virtues? May you also care about works of mercy, seizing every opportunity to do good. This will gradually take you away from your evil thoughts and from all sin; indeed, the more you enjoy life with God, the more you will hate sin.

1.9.0.en: In the beginning: the time of the beginning of the creation of the world.

1.9.1.en: The Divine inspiration affirmed in (Ps 102:25-27) the attribute of creation in the Lord Christ, and this is evidence of the oneness of the Father and the Son, because God alone is the Creator, and David called Him “O Lord,” affirming His divinity. In this psalm he speaks about Christ, the Savior of mankind, who is the Creator of the whole world, heaven with all the angels and creatures in it, and earth with all the people and beings on it.

1.10.0.en: The psalm declares that all creatures will pass away on the last day, and likens them to a garment which by its nature wears out and decays when time passes over it. It also likens creatures to a vesture that God folds up, so that it becomes a piece of cloth that is no longer used; but Christ, on the other hand, is not touched by change, for He is eternal and created all these creatures at a particular time, the time He created the world, and He lives forever. Thus the superiority of Christ over the angels and all creatures appears.

1.11.0.en: My right hand: it signifies power and perfect divine glory, for God has neither right nor left.

1.11.1.en: Thine enemies: all who refuse to believe in you and become against you.

1.11.2.en: The psalm (110:1) declares the Father's words to the Son after He accomplished redemption, saying, “The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand,” that is, to you belongs all power and you are established in it, and everyone who opposes you is subject to you. This is unique to Christ alone and cannot be said of any angel, because he is a creature, whereas Christ is God, all-powerful and almighty.

1.12.0.en: Because the Lord Christ is seated on the throne, He has authority over all the angels to send them as created spirits to serve and attend to the needs of the people who have resolved to live with Him and to enjoy the inheritance of eternal life. Christ is God, whereas the angels are His servants.

1.12.1.en: Yes, heavenly Love, the God who entrusted my salvation, mine the sinner, to no one but His only Son. What love is this, my God, with which You loved me, so that You set Yourself apart for my sake, reigning in my heart with uprightness and righteousness and the hatred of iniquity, founding and establishing the earth for me to walk upon, and then declaring to me: do not cling to it or be attached to it, for it perishes and passes away. You send Your angels to serve me, who long for Your salvation. Beloved, grant me a heart overflowing with thanksgiving for Your boundless graces in the person of Your Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, that I may live rejoicing and glad in You here on earth until I reach perfect rejoicing in heaven.

1.12.2.en: A comparison between Christ and the angels as it appears in (Heb 1). Aspect: the Lord Christ; the angels. The comparison. Nature: one with the Father in essence; luminous spirits. “Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee” (v. 5); “Who maketh his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire” (v. 7); “I will be to him a Father, and he shall be to me a Son” (v. 5); “ministering spirits” (v. 14). Worship: Christ is the One worshipped by the angels; the angels offer worship to God. “And let all the angels of God worship him” (v. 6). Creator: Christ is the Creator; created spirits like the rest of nature. “By whom also he made the worlds” (v. 2); “Who maketh his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire” (v. 7); “Thou, Lord (the Son), in the beginning hast laid the foundation of the earth; and the heavens are the works of thine hands” (v. 10); “ministering spirits” (v. 14). Eternity: Christ is eternal, begotten of the Father before all ages; the angels are created, having a beginning in time. “Who maketh his angels” (v. 7); “Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee” (v. 5). Righteousness: Christ is God the Righteous, free from all error in Himself; creatures liable to error, as proved by the fall of some of them, who are the demons.

1.12.3.en: “Thou hast loved righteousness, and hated iniquity” (v. 9). Authority: Christ has all the authority that God has; the angels are sent by God for service. “But to which of the angels said he at any time, Sit on my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool?” (v. 13); “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent forth to minister” (v. 14). Constancy: Christ, to Him be glory, is constant and does not change, and is eternal in Himself; for the angels, their constancy is from God, and their immortal and eternal life is a gift from God.

1.12.4.en: “They shall perish; but thou remainest” (v. 11); “Thou art the same, and thy years shall not fail” (v. 12). The incarnate Christ our Savior. St. Paul continues the discourse that came in the first chapter and draws from it an important application, which is to give heed to the salvation that was accomplished on the Cross. Then he begins to prove the necessity of the appearance of the Lord Christ in this humble form, that is, lower than the angels, for the sake of our salvation.
